extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and critical thinking
extracted.subtask_description: Recognizing and evaluating common fallacies in inductive and deductive reasoning (analogies, generalizations, syllogisms, ambiguity) and assessing whether premises, terms, and inferred relations legitimately support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: False analogy / improper inference from analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer that because two things are similar in many respects, a disputed property holds in both; especially avoid analogies where the point essential to the inference (e.g., dependence on scarcity vs usefulness) differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that in the two cases asserted to be analogous the same law is really operating; there must be a causal connection between the known resemblance and the inferred one. Beware metaphors and remote analogies: the applicability of the metaphor/analogy is the very thing to be made out. Examples: inferring that metropolis growth is a disease from analogy with an animal heart; Pythagorean numerical analogies; coins vs commodities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor is not proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor or figurative illustration does not prove a proposition; it usually asserts that an argument exists or aids apprehension, but cannot substitute for demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to clarify or suggest grounds of a claim, not as evidence. An apt metaphor may point to the means by which a fact could be proved, but its mere vividness does not establish logical parity (example: agricultural metaphors for education). Conversely, metaphors with no parity of causal basis (Bacon's river/works example) are misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad classification leads to false generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization from a class is misleading when the class groups together heterogeneous things that lack common properties significant enough to warrant general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the predicate used to group items denotes a consistent, verifiable property across members. Avoid extending a familiar word by 'slight links' to cases lacking the core fact (Bacon's critique of 'humidum'). Check that the abstraction is not 'temere et inæqualiter à rebus abstracta'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syllogistic rules to expose hidden fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratiocinative (deductive) fallacies are often revealed by formally setting out the argument as a syllogism; the syllogistic rules protect against many obvious fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If premises are explicitly stated and organized, errors (e.g., undistributed middle, illicit processes) become apparent. The exercise forces a reasoner to commit to the full set of premises required to defend a conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper conversion of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not convert universal affirmative propositions or hypothetical propositions improperly (e.g., from 'All A are B' infer 'All B are A'; from 'If A then B' infer 'If B then A').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the proper converse of a hypothetical is: If the consequent be false, the antecedent is false. Avoid treating a true conclusion as proof of the premises (mistaking direction of implication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing contraries and contradictories
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking the contrary of a proposition for its contradictory (or vice versa) leads to errors; contraries can both be false, while contradictories cannot both be true or both false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate habit of distinguishing contrary vs contradictory propositions; force ambiguous thought into explicit form to detect this error (helps avoid mistaking reverse of wrong for right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious syllogism: more than three terms / undistributed middle / illicit process
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogisms fail when they covertly contain more than three terms, have an undistributed middle term, or commit illicit processes of the extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the terms and their distribution; require the explicit statement of suppressed premises. While one can often save an argument by introducing a false premise, the syllogistic form shows what must be defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing premises between linked inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A chain of argument may commit a fallacy by altering the premises between one syllogism and the next — i.e., founding a later argument on a different (often insufficiently similar) proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the same proposition (with its qualifications) is actually carried forward; inspect whether any necessary qualification or limiting condition has been dropped between steps (examples: à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter).

rubrics_metrics.name: À dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter (losing qualifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: A common fallacy where a proposition true only with a qualification (secundum quid) is used as if it were true absolutely (simpliciter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify implicit conditions that make a premise true (time, circumstances, competitors' behavior). Examples: Mercantile theory (increase of money as increase of riches) ignoring necessary provisos; tithe/rent examples; individual vs collective interest in land use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of abstract truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles true 'in the abstract' (assuming absence of modifying causes) are mistaken for universally and absolutely true when used to derive concrete conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying an abstract maxim, ask what modifying causes were suppressed and whether they could exist in the actual case. The error is frequent in political and social reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dropping time or other conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to account for temporal conditions or other provisos (e.g., 'prices always find their level' misunderstood as 'are always at their level').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a proposition is about processes over time or instantaneous states; explicitly include time-conditions when they are essential to the truth of a premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity / equivocation (fallacy of ambiguous terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term used in different senses in premises and conclusion (or as an ambiguous middle) produces apparent but invalid inferences; the fallacy arises from an indistinct, fluctuating conception of what the evidence is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and eliminate equivocation by fixing meanings of key terms across the argument. Watch for ambiguous middles, changes of sense between premises and conclusion, and alternative grammatical/conceptual senses (examples: 'money' meaning currency vs capital; 'church' meaning clergy vs whole body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacia figuræ dictionis / paronymous-word fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that paronymous (grammatically related) words have precisely corresponding meanings (e.g., 'murder' vs 'murderer', 'presume' vs 'presumption').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve meaning when varying grammatical forms for convenience; do not infer that adjectival or verbal relatives carry the same evaluative force or implication as the substantive (examples: 'project' vs 'projector'; 'presumption' as slight suspicion vs 'to presume' as belief).

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymology fallacy (using original/etymological sense incorrectly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing that a modern usage must correspond to an etymological or 'strict' original sense (e.g., claiming 'representative' must mean mere spokesman because of the verb 'represent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect law, custom, and current usage that fix meanings; do not privilege etymology over established or contextual senses of a term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ambiguity leading to policy error
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical or political discourse, ambiguous phrases (e.g., 'influence of property', 'scarcity of money') can be used to conflate distinct concepts and mislead reasoning about policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify which sense of an ambiguous phrase is intended before drawing policy conclusions; distinguish persuasive influence from coercive influence, currency from loan-capital, etc., because conflation produces fallacious inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require explicit premises rather than relying on implied inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Many errors stem from suppressed or forgotten reasons that originally limited a premise; argument quality improves by making all premises explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exposed to an argument, restate it with all assumed and supporting premises. This practice reveals hidden conditions, qualifications, and potential faults (it is the value of forcing syllogistic form).
